name: Tolman's Fluid Sphere, Solution VII
description: A static star of perfect fluid whose density falls as the square of the radius, $\rho = \rho_c(1 - r^2/R^2)$ where the surface is empty. It is the seventh of the eight solutions Richard Tolman wrote down in 1939, and the density inside a neutron star follows it closely.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The first days of 1939 found Richard Tolman in Pasadena with neutron stars on his mind. He had been talking with Fritz Zwicky, a colleague at the California Institute of Technology, who had proposed Schwarzschild's star of constant density as a model for a "collapsed neutron star," and with J. Robert Oppenheimer and George Volkoff of the University of California, who were integrating the equations for a star of cold neutrons numerically [tolman1939]. Tolman wanted solutions he could write down in known functions, and for a sphere of fluid he knew of only two, Einstein's static universe and Schwarzschild's interior [tolman1939]. The journal received his paper on 3 January and printed it on 15 February, with Oppenheimer and Volkoff's right behind it [tolman1939, oppenheimer1939].¶Start from an equation of state, and the field equations have to be integrated numerically [tolman1939]. Tolman worked backwards: he chose a simple form for one of the two metric functions, picked so that the equations integrate by hand, and read the pressure and the density off afterwards [tolman1939]. He admitted the risk of "obtaining solutions which may not be physically interesting or even physically possible" [tolman1939]. Eight solutions came out, three already known and five new [tolman1939].¶For the seventh he assumed $g^{rr} = 1 - r^2/R^2 + 4r^4/A^4$, with $R$ and $A$ two constant lengths [tolman1939]. Its density is $8\pi G\rho/c^2 = 3/R^2 - 20r^2/A^4$, greatest at the centre and falling as the square of the radius [tolman1939]. Its pressure is a square root times the cotangent of a logarithm, and Tolman judged that its dependence on $r$ "is so complicated that the solution is not a convenient one for physical considerations" [tolman1939]. He worked through solutions IV, V, and VI in detail [tolman1939].¶The solution was found again and went under other names, the Durgapal and the Mehra solutions among them [raghoonundun2015]. Then M. S. R. Delgaty and Kayll Lake, in 1998, put 127 published solutions for a static sphere of fluid through six tests by computer algebra: an isotropic pressure, a regular centre, a positive pressure and density there, a surface where the pressure vanishes, a pressure and a density that fall outward, and sound slower than light [delgaty1998]. Sixteen passed, and in nine of those the speed of sound also falls outward [delgaty1998]. Tolman's seventh is one of the nine [delgaty1998].¶Does any star look like it? Sixty two years on, James Lattimer and Madappa Prakash computed neutron stars heavier than 1.2 solar masses from a wide variety of equations of state and plotted the density inside each against the radius: the curves follow $\rho = \rho_c(1 - r^2/R^2)$, which is Tolman's seventh solution with the density brought to zero at the surface [lattimer2001]. They remarked that it "is often overlooked in the literature," and wrote it out in the star's radius $R$ and its compactness $\beta = GM/(Rc^2)$ [lattimer2001]. From it they fitted the moment of inertia in units of $MR^2$, and expanded the binding energy in units of $M$, as functions of $\beta$ alone [lattimer2001]. The central pressure of the solution is infinite at $\beta \approx 0.3862$, and sound at the centre reaches the speed of light at $\beta \approx 0.2698$ [lattimer2001].¶Light can be caught inside such a star: that same year Nicholas Neary, Mustapha Ishak, and Lake found circular orbits of light within it for stars as large as $R \approx 3.2\,GM/c^2$, wider than the $3\,GM/c^2$ of Schwarzschild's photon sphere, and with sound still slower than light [neary2001]. The equation of state had to wait until 2015, when Ambrish Raghoonundun and David Hobill wrote the pressure as an explicit function of the density [raghoonundun2015]. They kept Tolman's second constant free through a number $\mu$, with $\rho = \rho_c(1 - \mu r^2/r_b^2)$ and $r_b$ the radius of the star: $\mu = 0$ is Schwarzschild's uniform star, $\mu = 1$ the star with an empty surface, and the values between are stars with a dense surface, whose equation of state resembles the bag model of quark matter [raghoonundun2015]. Four years later Nan Jiang and Kent Yagi gave the density one more parameter, and in most cases their profiles sit two to five times closer to those of computed neutron stars [jiang2019].

related.text: The equations of equilibrium for a star with any equation of state. Tolman's seventh solution satisfies them with $m = \beta r^3(5R^2 - 3r^2)/(2R^4)$, and Oppenheimer and Volkoff's paper follows his in the same issue [tolman1939, oppenheimer1939].

The star of uniform density, solution III on Tolman's list. His density $3/R^2 - 20r^2/A^4$ is uniform as $A \to \infty$, where $g^{rr}$ is Schwarzschild's $1 - r^2/R^2$ [tolman1939, raghoonundun2015].
The vacuum outside the star. At the surface the pressure vanishes and $g_{tt} = -(1 - 2\beta)$, so the metric continues as Schwarzschild's with $r_s = 2\beta R$ [lattimer2001].

The static star of the same year with no pressure along its radius, held up by the circular orbits of its particles. Tolman's fluid presses equally in every direction, and his paper was received on 3 January 1939, Einstein's on 10 May [tolman1939, einstein1939].
Richard Tolman's other spacetime, dust expanding or collapsing in spherical symmetry with a density that varies with radius, from 1934 [tolman1934].

Tolman's fifth and sixth solutions at $n = 1/2$, stars whose density and pressure are infinite at the centre in the ratio that holds for radiation. Grown without limit, both approach one metric, which he suggested "might be called the blackbody radiation solution" [tolman1939].

coordinates.name: Lattimer-Prakash

parameters.description: Radius of the star, where the density and the pressure both vanish and Schwarzschild's vacuum begins
Schwarzschild radius of the star, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ with $M$ its mass; the central pressure is finite for $r_s < 0.7724\,R$
Compactness of the star, $\beta = GM/(Rc^2)$, a pure number; the central density is $\rho_c = 15\beta c^2/(8\pi GR^2)$ and the density $\rho = \rho_c(1 - r^2/R^2)$
The component $g^{rr} = 1 - 2Gm(r)/(c^2r)$, with $m(r)$ the mass inside radius $r$; at the surface it is $1 - 2\beta$

The phase in $g_{tt}$, an angle, with $\partial_r\psi = -(r/R^2)\sqrt{3\beta/Z}$; it falls from the centre to $\arctan\sqrt{\beta/(3(1 - 2\beta))}$ at the surface, and the pressure is $p = (c^4/4\pi GR^2)\left(\sqrt{3\beta Z}\tan\psi - \beta(5 - 3r^2/R^2)/2\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use Lattimer and Prakash's form of the solution in coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The star has radius $R$ and mass $M$, with $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ and compactness $\beta = GM/(Rc^2)$. We write $Z$ for $g^{rr}$ and $\psi$ for the phase they call $\phi$, which is the azimuth here. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Tolman's Constants

parameters.description: Tolman's constant $R$, a length, which sets the central density, $8\pi G\rho_c/c^2 = 3/R^2$
Tolman's constant $A$, a length, which sets how fast the density falls, $8\pi G\rho/c^2 = 3/R^2 - 20r^2/A^4$; as $A \to \infty$ the density is uniform
Tolman's constant $B$, a pure number that scales $t$; the vacuum outside fixes it by $B^2\sin^2\psi = Z$ at the surface
Tolman's constant $C$, a pure number that shifts the phase $\psi$; it fixes the radius $r_b$ where the pressure vanishes
The component $g^{rr}$, Tolman's $e^{-\lambda}$, the form he assumed
Half the logarithm in Tolman's $g_{tt}$, with $\partial_r\psi = 2r/(A^2\sqrt{Z})$; the pressure is $8\pi Gp/c^4 = -1/R^2 + 4r^2/A^4 + (4\sqrt{Z}/A^2)\cot\psi$

coordinates.convention: We use Tolman's own form of the solution in coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The constants $R$, $A$, $B$, and $C$ are his, so $R$ is the length in the central density, $8\pi G\rho_c/c^2 = 3/R^2$, and the surface of the star is at $r = r_b$, where the pressure vanishes. We write $Z$ for $g^{rr}$ and $\psi$ for half the logarithm in his $g_{tt}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
